author: William Saville
reader_character: Jasper — adult first-person protagonist, externally they/them
title: The Night After the Show
subtitle: The Lanternweald — fourth expansion pass
content:
The last cable had tangled itself around Greg's ankle.

That was the only explanation I could find for why a man who had spent decades handling concert equipment was standing in the middle of Starwake Pier looking personally betrayed by a length of black cord.

"I swear it wasn't like that when I put it down," he said.

I looked at the knot.

"Maybe the cable has a private life."

"Very funny."

"It could be ethically non-monogamous. Perhaps it's seeing the speaker cable and the microphone stand."

He laughed so hard he had to lean against the equipment case.

"Don't tell me you're jealous of a cable."

"Only of how much attention you're giving it."

He grinned and reached for my hand, but the cable tightened around his boot.

"Hold that thought."

I bent down and unwound the loop.

The Listening Fair had ended an hour earlier. The crowd was gone, the tea table had been cleaned, and the donation box had been counted with Mara present. The temporary lights were off except for the safety lanterns along the accessible path.

We had agreed to finish the cleanup before leaving.

Greg had agreed very enthusiastically.

Now he was trying to make an enemy out of electrical equipment.

"Maybe you should write a song about it," I said.

"I already have three verses."

"Of course you do."

He hummed something ridiculous as we packed the cables. I joined in with a deliberately awful harmony. His smile grew until he couldn't keep the melody straight.

It was the kind of evening I liked best with him. No performance required, no audience expecting us to turn love into a single perfect story. Just the two of us, a lot of equipment, and the small satisfaction of work actually finished.

We carried the last case to the storage shed.

I checked the lock.

Greg checked it again.

"You're learning from Danse," I said.

"Hey, his system works."

"Only after we removed the part that needed a ladder."

Greg laughed.

We started toward the Starwake Door.

The night air was cool enough that I pulled my coat tighter. He noticed without making a fuss and offered me the spare scarf he'd brought. It was faded blue, soft from years of use, and smelled faintly of laundry soap.

"Thanks," I said.

"Always."

He slipped an arm around my shoulders as we walked.

For a while we didn't talk. The sound of the sea moved beneath the pier. Lanterns glowed along the path back to Lanternwell Square, where a few late visitors were making their way home from the other districts.

Then Greg stopped.

"Can I ask you something?"

"Of course."

"Are you happy?"

The question was so simple that I didn't know how to answer it.

"Right now?"

"Yeah. Right now."

I looked at him.

"I'm tired. My feet hurt. I have a notebook full of repairs we still need to schedule. And I'm happy."

He smiled.

"Good."

"Are you?"

"Yeah."

He looked toward the dark water.

"I used to think happy meant getting to the part after everything difficult. The concert's over, the money's enough, everybody's okay, nobody's upset."

"That sounds exhausting."

"It was."

He rubbed his thumb over my knuckles.

"Now I think it can just be this. A night where we did something good and still have a few problems to deal with tomorrow."

I leaned closer.

"That's a very nice way to say we have chores."

"Romantic, right?"

"Unbelievably."

He kissed my cheek.

I turned toward him.

"Was that all you had planned?"

He raised an eyebrow.

"I could do better."

"Could you?"

"Challenge accepted."

He kissed me properly this time, warm and slow, the kind that made the cold air feel less important. His hand rested lightly at my waist. I held the edge of his jacket and smiled against his mouth.

When we parted, he looked a little breathless.

"Better?"

"Much."

He grinned.

We went through the Starwake Door into Beach City, where the van waited beneath a streetlamp. The familiar smell of the coast met me: salt, asphalt, and somebody's late-night food from a nearby shop.

Greg opened the van and set down his guitar.

"Want to stay?"

"Yes."

He looked at me for another moment.

"Because you want to?"

"Because I want to."

He smiled, relief and affection moving together across his face.

Inside, we folded the blanket, put the equipment list on the dashboard, and made a small space where there had been too many things. Greg found a packet of crackers and offered them with great ceremony.

"A feast."

"Truly, you spoil me."

"I try."

We ate the crackers and laughed about the fair. He imitated Toph declaring the practice platform "almost competent." I tried to imitate Iroh's calm reply and failed because I started laughing halfway through the sentence.

Then the laughter settled.

Greg reached for my hand.

"I know you have other people you love," he said quietly. "I know we talked about ethical non-monogamy and polyamory, and I know it doesn't make tonight less ours."

I squeezed his fingers.

"It doesn't."

"I just wanted to say that I like having nights that belong to us because we choose them."

"Me too."

He leaned close.

The next kiss was unhurried. There was no need to fill the silence with a joke, though I knew he would if I asked. I rested my forehead against his and listened to the small sounds of the van cooling in the night.

"Stay with me," he whispered.

"I am."

We turned down the light and let the rest of the evening be private.

In the morning, sunlight came through the windshield and woke me before the alarm. Greg was still asleep, one hand resting near the folded equipment list. His hair looked as though it had been involved in a disagreement with a pillow.

I smiled.

I was tempted to let him sleep.

Then I remembered that the repair team was expecting the donation total by nine.

I nudged his shoulder.

"Greg."

A muffled sound.

"Greg, we have responsibilities."

"Tell them I'm a guitar."

"That makes no sense."

"Great guitars don't do paperwork."

I laughed.

He opened one eye.

"Coffee?"

"After the totals are sent."

"Brutal."

We made coffee anyway, then sat together at the small table outside the van and checked the ledger. The donations covered the new fasteners and some of the lumber, exactly as we'd announced. We sent the figures to Tamsin and copied the volunteers who had helped. No exaggeration. No promise that the rest of the repairs would happen by magic.

Greg looked at the final number.

"Not everything we wanted."

"No."

"Enough for the next step."

"Yes."

He leaned over and kissed my temple.

"Good morning."

"Good morning."

By the time we returned to Starwake Pier, the volunteers were already moving supplies to the safe storage area. Toph had left a note about checking the platform after the next rain. Iroh had sent a small tin of the new house tea blend as thanks.

We got to work.

That was the best part of the night after the show: the morning wasn't a punishment for being happy.

It was simply the next part of our life.
